opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the main reason is that the publicity was starting to distort what the award was supposed to mean. When I was at Tsinghua, the Special Scholarship had become this very high-profile event. There were big public defense sessions, lots of posts circulating on social media, and people would compare candidates almost like a competition show. On the surface that sounds exciting, but I think it created some unhealthy side effects.

First, it put a lot of pressure on students to package themselves. If you know your whole application is going to be dissected publicly, you start optimizing for what looks impressive to an outside audience: number of papers, venue names, titles, awards. That's not necessarily the same as doing deep, meaningful research. A student who spent three years on one hard problem with an uncertain outcome can look "weaker" on paper than someone who accumulated many incremental results. Heavy publicity amplifies that bias.

Second, it created an atmosphere of comparison that wasn't good for the broader student body. When only around ten people get it each year and everyone is watching, many other excellent students end up feeling like they're failures by comparison. Research is a long game, and people develop at different speeds. Some of the most interesting researchers I know were late bloomers. Making one award the center of attention sends the message that there's a single ladder everyone should climb.

Third, for the winners themselves, it's not always a blessing. Suddenly you have a label attached to you very early in your career, and people expect you to live up to it. That can make you more risk-averse, because you feel you have a reputation to protect. Good research often requires being willing to try things that might not work.

So I think lowering the volume is healthier. The scholarship can still recognize excellent students and give them support, but it returns to being an honor rather than a spectacle. Students can focus on what they actually care about, rather than on how their profile will look in a public vote or a viral article. In the end, the value of the work should speak for itself over the long run, not through how loudly it gets promoted at one moment.

r001.rationale: The response says students develop at different speeds and that there should not be a single ladder, but it does not state that diverse student pursuits make it difficult to identify Tsinghua’s ten best undergraduates by one standard.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the Special Scholarship was always meant to recognize students, not to turn them into celebrities. When the award ceremony became this huge public event, with livestreams and widely circulated stories about each winner, the attention shifted away from the work itself and onto the persona. For the winners, that kind of spotlight at twenty or twenty-one can be distorting. You start getting labeled as a "god" or a "genius," and suddenly you're expected to live up to a narrative that was written for you by others. That's a lot of pressure, and honestly it can make people more cautious about taking risks, because failure now feels public.

For everyone else on campus, the effect was arguably worse. Most students are never going to win that award, and watching a handful of peers being celebrated like that every year reinforced a very narrow definition of success. It encouraged people to chase the metrics they thought the committee was looking for, which doesn't lead to good research or a healthy learning environment.

So when the school dialed down the publicity, I think it sent the right message. The recognition still exists, the support still exists, but it's quieter and it's about the substance. Those of us who went through it can just get back to doing the work, and students who didn't win don't have to measure themselves against a spectacle. To me, that's a healthier version of what the scholarship was supposed to be in the first place.

r001.rationale: The response criticizes a narrow definition of success and students chasing award metrics, but does not state that students’ varied pursuits make it difficult to identify the ten best undergraduates by one standard.

astra-6.text: I think the scholarship should be an encouragement, rather than something that turns students into public symbols of success. Too much publicity can make it seem as though there’s one standard for what an outstanding student should look like, and it can put pressure on both the recipients and their peers. Reducing that attention leaves more room for students to follow their own interests. The recognition still matters, but it doesn’t need to define a person.

r001.rationale: The response says publicity can imply a single standard for an outstanding student and that students should follow their own interests, but it does not state that the diversity of Tsinghua students’ pursuits makes it difficult to identify the university’s ten best undergraduates.
